rows.timeline_year_basis: The Qur'an is never dated; it is the single starting block
rows.name: Qur'an
rows.detail: Explicit: 'qard hasan' appears in six verses, always a loan 'to Allah'; 2:282 governs recording debts.
rows.detail_long: Who: The Qur'an is the first rung of every USUL ladder: it is never dated, and every later rung refers back to it. What: The goodly-loan phrase runs through 2:245, 5:12, 57:11, 57:18, 64:17 and 73:20 — spending framed as a loan God repays manifold — while 2:282 commands writing debts down. The verses, in the translation held in the Gold Ark Library: 2:245 — “Who is it that would loan Allah a goodly loan so He may multiply it for him many times over? And it is Allah who withholds and grants abundance, and to Him you will be returned.” 57:11 — “Who is it that would loan Allah a goodly loan so He will multiply it for him and he will have a noble reward?” 57:18 — “Indeed, the men who practice charity and the women who practice charity and [they who] have loaned Allah a goodly loan - it will be multiplied for them, and they will have a noble reward.” 64:17 — “If you loan Allah a goodly loan, He will multiply it for you and forgive you. And Allah is Most Appreciative and Forbearing.” Why here: The Qur'an opens the Qard ladder and is never dated. Source: Qur'an 2:245; 5:12; 57:11; 57:18; 64:17; 73:20; 2:282.

rows.name: Sahih Bukhari 2068
rows.detail: The Prophet borrowed on credit against his pledged armor — borrowing itself as prophetic practice.
rows.detail_long: Who: Sahih al-Bukhari was compiled by Imam al-Bukhari (810-870), the most celebrated hadith scholar in Sunni Islam; it is widely regarded as the most authentic collection after the Qur'an. Narrator: Aisha. What: The same Aisha narration that anchors rahn shows the Prophet as borrower: credit taken, security given, debt honored. Graded Sahih. The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library: “We mentioned about pledging in Salam trade to Ibrahim, Aswad, with reference to Hadrat Aishah , narrated a Hadith to me: The Prophet (ﷺ) purchased food grains from a Jew on credit and mortgaged his iron armor to him.” It stands in Sales and Trade. Why here: 'Prophet's sayings (hadith)' rung of the Qard ladder; shown at 610 (no dated record; placed at the start of the Prophetic period (610)). Source: Sahih Bukhari 2068.

rows.name: Sunan Ibn Majah 2430
rows.detail: 'No Muslim lends to another Muslim twice but it counts as charity once' — graded Da'eef.
rows.detail_long: Who: Sunan Ibn Majah was compiled by Ibn Majah al-Qazwini (824-887); it is the last of the six canonical Sunni hadith collections. Narrator: Qais bin Rumi (via Ibn Mas'ud). What: The lending-virtue narration via Ibn Mas'ud (the Sulaiman bin Udhunan story). Its grading is Da'eef — kept as ethics support, not legal proof. The report (opening), as held in the Gold Ark Library: ““Sulaiman bin Udhunan lent 'Alqamah one thousand Dirham until he got his salary, When he got his salary, he demanded that he pay him back and treated him harshly. He paid him back, and it was as if 'Alqamah was angry. Several months passed then he came to him and said: 'Lend me one thousand Dirham until my salary comes.' He said 'Yes, it would be an honor. O Umm 'Utbah! [...]” It stands in The Chapter on Charity. Why here: 'Prophet's sayings (hadith)' rung of the Qard ladder; shown at 610 (no dated record; placed at the start of the Prophetic period (610)). Source: Sunan Ibn Majah 2430.

rows.name: Bulugh al-Maram 1024
rows.detail: Guaranteed loan vs borrowed object. 'Is it a loan with a guarantee of return, or a borrowed object to be returned?' — the Prophet distinguishes the two liabilities by name.
rows.detail_long: Who: Bulugh al-Maram is one of the hadith collections held in the Gold Ark Library. Narrator: Ya'la bin Umaiya. What: The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library: asked for thirty coats of armor, Ya'la asks whether they are a guaranteed loan (madmunah) or a borrowed object ('ariyah) to be returned; the Prophet answers: a borrowed object that must be returned. The earliest-corpus articulation that LOAN and LENT-OBJECT are distinct liability types — the conceptual boundary classical qard doctrine builds on. The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library: “Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said to me, "When my messengers come to you, give them thirty coats of armor." I asked, "O Allah's Messenger, is it a loan with a guarantee (of its return), or a borrowed object that must be returned?" He replied, "No, it is a borrowed object that must be returned." .” It stands in Business Transactions. Why here: 'Prophet's sayings (hadith)' rung of the Qard ladder; shown at 622 (dated 622-632 (Madinan period); shown at the earliest year). Source: Bulugh al-Maram 1024.

rows.name: Ibn Abbas (attrib., Tanwir al-Miqbas)
rows.detail: The earliest attributed gloss on 2:245: the 'goodly loan' as sincere charity, revealed about Abu'l-Dahdah of the Ansar.
rows.detail_long: Who: Abd Allah ibn Abbas (618-686) was a cousin of the Prophet Muhammad, remembered as the 'Scholar of the Umma' and highly regarded for his knowledge of traditions and his interpretation of the Qur'an. The commentary Tanwir al-Miqbas is attributed to him by tradition; the attribution is traditional, not critical, which is why the work is marked 'attrib.' What: Tanwir al-Miqbas on 2:245: lending to Allah = giving 'in charity sincerely wanting nothing but the sake of Allah', rewarded 'a thousand times', with the revelation-occasion naming Abu'l-Dahdah of the Helpers. The word qard enters the tradition wearing its benevolence meaning first. Attribution traditional, not critical — hence 'attrib.' Why here: 'Qur'an commentary (tafsir)' rung of the Qard ladder; shown at 687 (death of Ibn Abbas, to whom the work is attributed). Source: Tanwir al-Miqbas (attrib. Ibn Abbas), on Q2:245.

rows.name: Ibn Kathir
rows.detail: Ibn Kathir on 57:11 and 64:17: the loan 'to Allah' as charitable spending with guaranteed manifold repayment.
rows.detail_long: Who: Ibn Kathir (1301-1373) of Damascus was a Qur'an commentator, historian and scholar, an expert in tafsir, history and fiqh. A Shafi'i, he is known for a commentary that takes a critical approach to Isra'iliyyat (stories taken from earlier communities). What: Ibn Kathir's treatments of 57:11 and 64:17 read the 'goodly loan to Allah' as charitable spending repaid manifold — with the narrations of Ibn Mas'ud and Abu'd-Dahdah giving his garden against a date-palm in Paradise. The theological frame that makes interest-free lending worship. Why here: 'Qur'an commentary (tafsir)' rung of the Qard ladder, Shafi'i voice; shown at 1373 (year of the author's death). Source: Tafsir Ibn Kathir, on Q57:11.

rows.name: Mufti Muhammad Shafi Usmani
rows.detail: Ma'ariful Qur'an on 2:245: the 'loan to Allah' is figurative — AND real lending to His slaves in their hour of need is itself credited with great merit.
rows.detail_long: Who: Mufti Muhammad Shafi Usmani (1897-1976) was born in Deoband, became chief mufti of Darul Uloom Deoband in 1931, and later Grand Mufti of Pakistan in Karachi. His best-known work, Ma'ariful Qur'an, is an Urdu commentary on the whole Qur'an that began as a decade of weekly radio lectures. He belonged to the Hanafi school and the Deobandi movement. What: Ma'ariful Qur'an on 2:245: 'loan' figuratively means spending in Allah's way, surely returned like a loan — a date given grows past Mount Uhud — and the verse has ALSO been read as actual lending to human beings, 'thereby helping them in their hour of need... credited with great merit in Hadith'. The modern mufassir holding both readings together: charity AND the interest-free loan. Why here: 'Qur'an commentary (tafsir)' rung of the Qard ladder, Hanafi voice; shown at 1976 (year of the author's death). Source: Ma'ariful Qur'an, on Q2:245.

rows.name: Classical consensus (four schools)
rows.work_title: Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali fiqh manuals
rows.detail: Universal from the earliest fiqh: qard is gratuitous; ANY stipulated increase is riba; repay exactly the principal.
rows.detail_long: What: No school ever wavered: the loan contract admits no stipulated benefit to the lender — the bright line that makes qard the anti-interest contract. Year set at 795 (earliest surviving school literature, Malik's Muwatta) as the recording point. In the work itself (vol. and page 7:394; our literal translation from the Arabic): “(As for) its pillar, it is the offer and the acceptance; and the offer is the lender's saying: I have lent you this thing, or: take this thing as a loan, and the like of that.” It also states: “So it is determined that what is obligatory in it is the return of the like; so its permissibility is specific to what has a like.” It also states: “And because the stipulated increase resembles riba; because it is an excess that no counter-value stands against; and guarding against real riba, and against the semblance of riba, is obligatory.” Why here: 'Classical law schools' rung of the Qard ladder; shown at 795 (standard references). Source: Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali fiqh manuals.

Between points 2 and 3 the page cites: «نَهَى عَنْ قَرْضٍ جَرَّ نَفْعًا» ("he forbade a loan that draws a benefit"), introduced as narrated from the Messenger of God. rows.name: AAOIFI
rows.detail: AAOIFI Shari'ah Standard No. 19 (Qard), adopted 2004: microfinance, current accounts; voluntary extra repayment allowed if unstipulated.
rows.detail_long: Who: AAOIFI (the Accounting and Auditing Organization for Islamic Financial Institutions) issues the Shari'ah Standards. They are mandatory in Bahrain, its home jurisdiction, and adopted in the UAE and other countries. What: SS19 keeps the classical rule and adds banking detail. Adoption: 19 May 2004. Clauses read in the standard's text: 4/1 stipulated excess = riba in any form (quality, quantity, benefit, written or customary); 5/2 voluntary excess at repayment permissible if not stipulated or customary; 7 no tying a sale or lease to the qard; 9/1-9/2 service charges limited to actual direct costs, method set by the Shari'ah Supervisory Board, indirect costs excluded; 10/1/1 current accounts are loans. Why here: 'Modern rules & standards' rung of the Qard ladder; shown at 2004 (adopted Shari'ah Board meeting 12, Al-Madinah, 26-30 Rabi' I 1425 / 15-19 May 2004). Source: AAOIFI Shari'ah Standard No. 19 (Qard).
